newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: 100,000 in streets as anti-Milosevic protest grows.
newsitem.headline: 100,000 in streets as anti-Milosevic protest grows.

text.p: At least 100,000 opposition supporters accusing the government of election fraud marched in Belgrade on Saturday as part of a campaign to try to oust Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.
They pelted the building of the state-controlled Serbian television with fruit and eggs and threw smoke bombs, but stewards ensured there was no violence.
The number of protesters, including parents with young children, grew despite doubts that peaceful demonstrations could break Milosevic's grip on power.

Student leaders urged their followers, marching up to 20 abreast through city centre streets and gathering more supporters as they went, to avoid giving Milosevic any excuse to intervene with riot police.
Large reserves of police were marshalled in the city but stayed out of sight as the two-week protest continued.
One mother said she brought her children "because I want them to learn what democracy is...I want them to remember this."
The demonstrations are the longest sustained popular challenge to Milosevic's nine-year rule, during which he has presided over the break-up of former Yugoslavia and wars with Croatia and Bosnia.

But political sciences student Aleksander Kricic appeared to speak for many marchers when he told reporters: "I'm sorry we're not getting more support from taxi drivers and other workers. When they protested we supported them."
Another student who identified himself only as Nikola said: "Personally I think nothing can change in this peaceful way. But we have to maintain order. We will not give in to provocations."

The protests followed a claim by the Zajedno (Together) coalition of opposition parties that Milosevic's socialists robbed them of victory in local elections which would have given them control of the capital and other cities.
The protests have been peaceful in recent days after the buildings of Serbian television and Politika newspaper, another socialist mouthpiece, were damaged by stoning.
With both sides bidding for the support of the wider public in Serbia, the opposition and student leaders want to deprive the authorities of any opportunity to accuse them of violence.

They have been made vulnerable since Zajedno leader Danica Draskovic was heard telling reporters she would like to see the emergence of terrorism as Zajedno claimed the election fraud showed that Milosevic could not be removed by fair elections.
The socialists annulled Zajedno victories in the local elections and organised new votes which returned the socialists to power.
Opposition parties are threatening to boycott parliament and local councils unless Serbia's parliament cancels the disputed election results when it meets on Tuesday.
A boycott would have little practical effect because the socialists control the republican and federal parliaments.
But opposition leaders believe it would underscore their campaign to convince the world that Milosevic runs a one-party state despite the appearance of multi-party democracy in Yugoslavia.
Diplomats said Milosevic, whose police force has kept a low profile, hoped the demonstration campaign across the country would run out of steam.
Privately Zajedno officials agree that they will probably not win any substantial victory, but insist their tactics have uncovered cracks in his power.
"We have torn off his mask in front of the world to show him as he really is -- a small-time Balkan dictator unable to bear the slightest defeat," Zajedno leader Zoran Djindjic said.
